You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Ceramic capacitors, although promising for advanced high-power energy storage, face challenges in energy density and efficiency at high temperatures, which restrict their practical applications. Guided by phase field simulations, we propose a structural design strategy to construct weakly coupled polar nanoclusters in superparaelectric state, and fabricate BaTiO3-based multilayer ceramic capacitors via prototype device technology. The capacitors achieve an ultra high energy storage density of 19.0 J·cm-3 and a high energy storage efficiency of 95.5% at room temperature. More importantly, both metrics are still on the order of >10.0 J·cm-3 and >95.0%, respectively, over 25-160 oC, outperforming previously reported ceramic capacitors. The weak coupling between adjacent nanoclusters caused by disordered polar configurations, suppresses nonlinear polarization response and temperature sensitivity, ultimately enabling superior energy storage performance, which is confirmed by atomic-scale microstructure analysis. This work advances next-generation electronics and provides insights for developing high-performance high-temperature ceramic capacitors.

---

## Introduction

Lead-free ceramic capacitors have emerged as a key component for applications in portable electronics, electric vehicles, and large-scale energy storage systems due to their significant advantages, including eco-friendliness and ultra-high power density, which enable ultra-fast charging and discharging rates, as well as high voltage tolerance and reliability 1–3. However, compared to batteries and electrochemical capacitors, relatively low recoverable energy density (Wrec) and efficiency (η) limit their potential to meet practical requirements for miniaturization and integration 4–6. In order to meet the requirements of practical applications, ceramic dielectric capacitors must feature extremely slim polarization-electric field (P-E) loops and high field-induced polarization 7,8. However, achieving high polarization often leads to significant hysteresis effects, and vice versa 9,10. In response to this challenge, researchers employed various strategies to engineer the transition from ferroelectrics (FEs) to relaxor ferroelectrics (RFEs) and have made significant progress 11,12. This transition destroys the long-range ordered, strongly coupled micron-scale FE domains, resulting in lower polarization switching energy barriers and enhanced η value of ceramic capacitors 13,14. According to numerous reported ceramic systems, the BaTiO3-x(Na0.5Bi0.5)TiO3 (0≤x≤1, BT-100xNBT) RFEs have attracted significant attention due to its significant tetragonal distortions with varying composition and high spontaneous polarization 15–17. For instance, through precise local structural design in BT-50NBT-based RFEs, an exceptionally high energy density (>10 Jcm−3) and energy efficiency (>90%) have been achieved 18. Unfortunately, the Wrec value of this ceramic at a high temperature of 150°C is sharply decreased to approximately 8.5 Jcm−3, and the corresponding η is also reduced to around 85%. Temperature-sensitive energy storage performance and low high-temperature capacitance density (<10 Jcm−3) of recently reported lead-free ceramics still restrict their applicability at high-temperature conditions. For instance, the (Bi1/3Na1/6K1/6Ba1/6Sr1/6)(Ti0.8Zr0.2)O3 high-entropy ceramic exhibits an excellent energy storage density of 18.7 Jcm−3 at room temperature. However, its energy storage density notably drops below 10.0 Jcm−3 at 160°C 19. Similarly, the BaTiO3-(Bi0.5Na0.5)(Zn1/3Nb2/3)O3 system formed by multi-ion doping has an ultra high energy storage efficiency of 96.1%, but the insufficient thermal stability of energy storage density limits its applicability in a wide temperature range 20. Therefore, developing lead-free ceramic dielectric capacitors with high energy storage performance and excellent high-temperature stability is crucial for the next generation of dielectric capacitors that can operate stably under high electric fields and at temperatures up to 150°C.

Typical RFEs always exhibit small polarization hysteresis while suffering from early polarization saturation under sufficiently high external electric fields, restricting the rapid enhancement of energy storage performance when increasing the external electric field 21. Moreover, the energy storage performance of typical RFEs is often sensitive to temperature changes 22. From a thermodynamic perspective, domain size plays a crucial role in influencing the polarization response, encompassing long-range FE interactions and switching barriers. When sufficiently reducing the domain size and weakening the domain coupling, the polar state becomes easily redirectable, resulting in nearly zero polarization hysteresis and mitigated polarization saturation. Interestingly, as shown in Fig. 1a, this phenomenon can be observed in superparaelectric state within the temperature range of Tm < T < TB, where Tm is the peak temperature of the dielectric constant and TB represents the Burns temperature. In comparison to strongly coupled micro-domains and nano-domains, weakly coupled polar nanoclusters in superparaelectric state exhibit a super-fast and reversible response under loading and unloading the external electric field, which prevents the phenomenon of polarization hysteresis and premature polarization saturation, resulting in remarkable energy storage density and efficiency 21,23. In addition, these weakly coupled polar nanoclusters are insensitive to the variation of ambient temperature, and the corresponding dielectric constant remains stable over a broad temperature range, which is highly important for enhancing the thermal stability of energy storage performance 24,25.

Guided by phase-field simulations, as shown in Fig. 1b, the introduction of foreign ions such as Sr2+, La3+, and Zr4+ into the BT-35NBT matrix increases the local random field, disrupting long-range ordered, strongly coupled micro-domains and forming small weakly coupled polar nanoclusters. This configuration features rhombohedral (R) and tetragonal (T) polar nanoclusters embedded within cubic (C) paraelectric matrixes. Adjusting the ratio and distribution of polar and nonpolar states for R-, T-, and C-phases aims to minimize polarization hysteresis while maximizing maximum polarization. Such weakly coupled polar nanoclusters can exert a pinning effect that effectively inhibits local structural changes induced by atomic thermal vibration and thereby significantly enhances the stability of the phase structure over a wide temperature range. It is encouraging that the unique structural design enables the fabricated multilayer ceramic capacitors (MLCCs) to exhibit excellent energy storage performance not only at room temperature, but also over a wide temperature range. Even at a high temperature of 160°C, the Wrec remains greater than 10.0 J·cm-3, and the η exceeds 95.0%. This advancement provides a significant reference for developing next-generation high-temperature dielectric capacitors.

---

## Results

To uncover the underlying origin of the enhanced high-temperature energy storage performance of lead-free ceramic dielectrics induced by weakly coupled polar nanoclusters, the two-dimensional phase field simulation was used to study the correlation between the polar structure evolution and the corresponding hysteresis behavior of (1−x)[0.65BaTiO3-0.35(Na0.5Bi0.5)TiO3]-xSr0.7La0.2ZrO3 (SLZ100x, x=0, 0.05, 0.1, 0.15, 0.2) ceramics at different temperatures, as shown in Fig. 2a and Supplementary Fig. 1. The initial BT-35NBT ceramic features long-range ordered, strongly coupled T-phase domain structure, as substantiated by its P-E hysteresis loops with large polarization but high hysteresis loss. After introducing SLZ, as expected, the domains were transformed from macroscopic FE domains to nanodomains and subsequently to smaller weakly coupled polar nanoclusters, accompanied by increasingly slender P-E loops. This progression suggests that the introduction of SLZ effectively disrupts the long-range FE order in BT-35NBT ceramics. Simultaneously, the content of the T-phase decreases significantly, resulting in a disordered polarization structure with coexisting R-, T- and C-phases. The randomly distributed polar structure modifies local energy barriers, stabilizes the favorable polarization, and forms the unique structures with weakly coupled R and T polar nanoclusters divided by nonpolar C-phase over a broad temperature range, thereby enhancing temperature-insensitive energy storage performance. In addition, the weak coupling characteristic is responsible for excellent electric field response performance in the SLZ15 ceramic (Fig. 2b). In the initial state, benefiting from such a weak coupling effect, the polarization directions are highly randomly distributed. Upon the loading of external electric field, the polarizations rapidly reorient and align with the electric field direction. After the removal of external electric field, the polarization quickly deviates from the directional alignment state and eventually recovers its initial disordered distribution, demonstrating fast and reversible polarization response behavior. At the same time, optimizing the ratio and distribution of polar nanoclusters further reduces potential barriers for domain switching, enabling the flattest domain switching paths (Fig. 2c). Weakly coupled polar nanoclusters also promote the formation of random fields, which provides a strong driving force for the electric field-induced recovery of large domains to a multi-domain state (Fig. 2d). These results lead to a recoverable electric field-induced relaxor FE state and promote linear-like polarization behavior.

An aberration-corrected scanning transmission electron microscope was employed to investigate the atomic-scale structural characteristics of SLZx ceramics. Figure 3a, b shows the high-angle annular dark-field scanning transmission electron microscopy (HAADF-STEM) images for representative compositions of BT-35NBT and SLZ15 ceramics along [100]c direction. The polarization displacement vectors were computed through software simulation and presented by yellow arrows. Herein, the morphological structure is identified by observing the projected displacements of the B-site cations (Zr/Ti) relative to the four nearest A-site cations (Ba/Na/Bi/Sr) at the lattice center. Based on the 2D Gaussian peak fitting results, the larger domains can be observed by same arrow pointing for BT-35NBT ceramics (highlighted by the green arrow at the right of Fig. 3a). By contrast, local fluctuations are observed for the SLZ15 ceramic due to the disordered nature of the A-site cations. As a result, smaller weakly coupled polar nanoclusters of R- and T-phases are embedded within nonpolar C-phase matrixes (Fig. 3b). These results confirm that SLZx ceramics with weakly coupled polar nanoclusters were successfully fabricated under the guidance of phase-field simulations. The disordered and weakly coupled polar nanoclusters contribute to enhancing the stability of local structure and energy storage performance under temperature fluctuation 26. Additionally, as observed in the atomic-resolved energy-dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) mapping for the SLZ15 ceramic in Supplementary Fig. 2, the Ba, Bi, Na, La, and Sr elements are distributed in A-sites, while the Zr and Ti elements are distributed in B-sites, respectively. It promotes the destabilization of cation sites in the perovskite structure and induces the formation of weakly coupled polar nanoclusters. From the comparative distribution of pixel intensities of A- and B-site atomic columns between the BT-35NBT and SLZ15 ceramics, it can be concluded that multi-element doping significantly enhances the atomic-scale disorder of the ceramics (Fig. 3c–f). Significantly, the intensity fluctuation is more prominent at the A-site columns (Ba2+/Na+/Bi3+/Sr2+/La2+) in the SLZ15 ceramic, suggesting large random displacements of A-site cations. These random shifts directly generate strong local electric fields that disrupt long-range polar order. In contrast, the B-site (Ti4+/Zr4+) columns show small intensity variations. Nevertheless, their fluctuations exhibit high spatial correlation closely linked to cooperative displacements of B-site cations and tilting of oxygen octahedra. This correlated B-site behavior locally biases polarization directions and contributes to stabilizing nanoscale polar nanoclusters. According to the axial displacement data, the polarization angle and amplitude mapping of BT-35NBT and SLZ15 ceramics along the [100]c direction is illustrated in Supplementary Fig. 3. Compared to the BT-35NBT ceramic, the polarization angle and amplitude of the SLZ15 ceramic exhibit a markedly non-uniform random distribution. Meanwhile, this random distribution of T- and R-phase polar nanoclusters is isolated by nonpolar C-phase, facilitating a more rapid and efficient response to the external electric field 27. In addition, compared with the average c/a ratio of the BT-35NBT ceramic, that of the SLZ15 ceramic displays a noticeable decrease accompanied by a more pronounced discrete distribution (Supplementary Fig. 4). The variation of the c/a ratio indicates that as SLZ content increases, atomic disorder within the system escalates and lattice distortion intensifies, further enhancing the random field and effectively delaying polarization saturation 28.

X-ray diffraction (XRD, Supplementary Fig. 5) analysis confirms that all samples exhibit a pure perovskite phase. The pure BT-35NBT ceramic displays a characteristic T phase, evident from the distinct splitting of XRD peaks (002)/(200) 28,29. As the SLZ content increases, the (200) diffraction peak gradually shifts to a low angle, primarily due to the larger radius of the dopant ions (R(Sr2+)=1.44 Å, R(La3+)=1.06 Å, R(Zr4+)=0.79 Å), which results in lattice expansion. To further analyze the phase composition in the SLZx ceramics, Rietveld refinement was performed on the XRD data for each composition, as shown in Fig. 4a and Supplementary Fig. 6. The results indicate that the rhombohedral (R3c) and tetragonal (P4bm) phases coexist in the SLZ15 ceramic, with mass fractions of 56.2 wt% and 43.8 wt%, respectively. Notably, as the SLZ content increases, the proportion of the R-phase at room temperature increases monotonically, from 24.6 wt% at x=0.05–71.4 wt% at x=0.20. Both the R-phase and T-phase are polar phases with high polarization, which facilitates the achievement of a larger maximum polarization (Pmax) in ceramic dielectrics under the application of an external electric field 23.

To primarily confirm the designed SLZx ceramics in superparaelectric state near room temperature, the temperature dependence of dielectric constant and dielectric loss (tanδ) was analyzed (Supplementary Figs. 7 and 8). As the SLZ content increases, the tanδ exhibits a significant decreasing trend while remaining consistently below 0.01 across a broad temperature range from room temperature to 300°C, accompanied by the shift of Tm towards low temperatures from 184°C for x=0 to −83°C for x=0.20 at 1 kHz. Additionally, the relaxor diffusion factor γ, calculated using the modified Curie-Weiss law 30, tends to increase with the increment of x, indicating an improvement in relaxor properties (Supplementary Fig. 9). Based on the dielectric spectrum at 1 kHz, a possible composition-temperature phase diagram was constructed (Fig. 4b). The Tm significantly decreases with increasing SLZ content, facilitating the transition from relaxor FE to superparaelectric state. Consequently, the designed ceramics are fully situated in superparaelectric state from −56°C to 162°C when x=0.15, indicating the existence of weakly coupled polar nanoclusters over a broad temperature range. In addition, weakened coupling between the R-phase and T-phase polar nanoclusters significantly reduces the stress required for polarization reorientation in response to an external electric field, leading to lower strain vibration and potential failure risks 8,31.

The relaxation characteristics of SLZx ceramics were studied through the first-order reversal curve (FORC) distribution, as shown in Fig. 4c and Supplementary Fig. 10. The BT-35NBT ceramic displays a high-intensity distribution near the origin, indicative of strongly coupled FE domain switching at low electric fields, resulting in an overall increase in polarization 32. This inhomogeneous FORC intensity distribution reflects the typical characteristics of strong polarization nonlinearity in FE materials 33. In contrast, the FORC intensity of the SLZ15 ceramic is more uniform distributed across all electric fields, indicating decreased coercive fields, reduced FE nonlinearity, and a more dispersed polarization contribution 34. In addition, the representative samples of BT-35NBT and SLZ15 ceramics were selected to analyze further the dynamic response of domains by piezoelectric force microscopy (PFM) at various voltages and relaxation times (Supplementary Figs. 11 and 12). For the BT-35NBT ceramic, a strong domain-switching signal is observed at a low voltage of 10 V, whereas the domain-switching signal in the SLZ15 ceramic is weak at this voltage but becomes more pronounced with increasing voltage, suggesting that local random fields and highly dynamic polar nanoclusters are present in the SLZ15 ceramic. Weakly coupled polar nanoclusters require a higher electric field to achieve long-range polarization, which explains the reduced polarization saturation observed in the SLZ15 ceramic. Furthermore, after removing the voltage and allowing a relaxation time of 20 min, the BT-35NBT ceramic retains their original remarkable signals, while the domain-switching signals in the SLZ15 ceramic are barely detectable. These results indicate that the introduction of SLZ diminishes the domain size of the BT-35NBT ceramic and induces weakly coupled polar nanoclusters. This structural modulation yields negligible Pr by virtue of rapid reversible polarization response, while concurrently enhancing the overall energy storage performance.

For ceramic capacitors, the breakdown strength (Eb) significantly influences their operating electric field and energy storage density. Thus, the breakdown characteristics of SLZx ceramics were initially evaluated using the Weibull distribution function 35. All samples exhibit a linear relationship with a large shape parameter (β>10, Supplementary Fig. 13), indicating the reliability of the results and consistent quality of the ceramic samples. In fact, the Eb of ceramic dielectrics is influenced by various complex factors, such as band gap (Eg), grain size, and insulation properties 36,37. For SLZx ceramics, the Eg is significantly enhanced with increasing the SLZ content (Supplementary Fig. 14). Specifically, the values of Eg are enhanced monotonously from 3.12 eV for the SLZ5 ceramic to 3.18 eV for the SLZ20 ceramic, leading to a substantial increase in the Eb. In addition, the average grain size (Ga) and Eb exhibit a negative correlation in ceramic dielectrics 28,38. According to the measured SEM (Supplementary Fig. 15), the Ga was evaluated by NanoMeasurer software. The Ga exhibits a decreasing tendency, from 0.72 μm for the BT-35NBT ceramic to 0.43 μm for the SLZ20 ceramic. The smaller Ga is beneficial to achieving higher Eb. Despite the fact that the radius of impedance spectra for SLZx ceramics tends to decrease with increasing temperature, the higher SLZ content still contributes to a larger radius, indicating the enhancement of total resistivity and Eb at high temperatures (Supplementary Fig. 16). In addition, the distinct single peaks of Z” and M” can be observed for the BT-35NBT ceramic, but they do not coincide at the same frequency (Supplementary Fig. 17). This lack of overlap indicates electrical inhomogeneity. In contrast, the peaks of Z” and M” closely overlap at the same frequency for the SLZ15 ceramic, demonstrating that the introduction of SLZ into the BT-35NBT ceramic effectively improves the electrical homogeneity. This enhancement in electrical homogeneity also contributes to the increase in Eb 39.

To better evaluate the overall energy storage performance of the designed ceramics, the unipolar P-E loops were measured at their critical electric field (Supplementary Figs. 18 and 19), and the related capacitive energy storage performance of Wrec and η were calculated (Fig. 4d). Despite the Pmax of the BT-35NBT ceramic reaching 37.9 μCcm−2 at a low breakdown strength (Eb = 160 kVcm−1), while the remnant polarization (Pr) is as high as 23.8 μCcm−2, leading to low energy storage density and efficiency (Wrec = 1.7 Jcm−3, η=48.6%, Supplementary Fig. 18). By tailoring the polar nanocluster configuration, the values of Wrec and η were dramatically improved to be on the order of 9.2 ± 0.28 Jcm−3 and 91.6 ± 0.24% at x=0.15. It is due to the fact that the strongly coupled FE order of the BT-35NBT ceramic is disrupted, resulting in the formation of R- and T-phase weakly coupled polar nanoclusters isolated by nonpolar C-phase matrixes, which contributes to the rapid polarization response and slim P-E loops. Nevertheless, when excessive SLZ is introduced (e.g., at x=0.2), the formation of nonpolar C-phase becomes dominant. Consequently, the Pmax value at an electric field of 620 kVcm−1 drops to only 30.5 μCcm−2, and the Wrec ultimately decreases to 7.5 Jcm−3. These results indicate that the generation of weakly coupled polar nanoclusters and the alterations in nanocluster configuration significantly optimize the energy storage performance of lead-free ceramics. Compared to the traditional solid-state reaction process, the method of repeated rolling process (RRP) facilitates the refinement of grain size and enhances sintering uniformity, leading to the increased Eb of ceramic dielectrics 25,40. Therefore, SLZ15 ceramics were prepared via the RRP (SLZ15-RRP) using SLZ15 powder to further optimize their energy storage performance. Figure 4e illustrates the unipolar P-E loops of the SLZ15-RRP ceramic under different electric fields. Obviously, the Pr remains negligible and its value is as low as 0.9 μCcm−2 even at 780 kVcm−1. It is worth noting that an ultra-high Wrec of 13.6 Jcm−3, along with a near-ideal efficiency of 95.0%, can be achieved for the SLZ15-RRP ceramic. The reliability of the Eb is validated through Weibull distribution analysis, as shown in Supplementary Fig. 20. The β of the SLZ15-RRP ceramic is 17.34, indicating high reliability of the Eb. The calculated Eb is on the order of 782.9 kVcm−1, closely corresponding to the Eb obtained in P-E loops. Herein, the remarkable comprehensive energy storage performance in this study is primarily due to their weakly coupled polar nanoclusters, compact microstructure, and uniform and small grain size (Supplementary Fig. 21). Weakly coupled polar nanoclusters exhibit high sensitivity to external electric fields, which enables ceramic dielectrics to achieve near-ideal energy efficiency. Meanwhile, the refined grain size effectively inhibits electrical tree propagation and shortens their growth paths, thereby significantly enhancing the Eb, as shown in Fig. 4f and Supplementary Fig. 22.

Except for achieving high energy storage performance at room temperature, their stability under different conditions is also critical in practical applications. Therefore, over a broad temperature range from room temperature to 160°C, the P-E loops consistently maintain a slim shape and the variation of Wrec and η is less than 10.0% and 5.0%, respectively, at an electric field of 500 kVcm−1 (Fig. 4g and Supplementary Fig. 23). To further assess frequency adaptability, P-E loops of the SLZ15-RRP ceramic were tested over a frequency range of 1–100 Hz (Supplementary Fig. 24). Obviously, the Wrec remains stably at ~ 7.9 Jcm−3, and the η consistently stays above 94.0%, which indicates excellent frequency stability. Moreover, the energy storage performance of the SLZ15-RRP ceramic remains stable with a change rate of less than 2.0% in both Wrec and η after 106 cycles (Fig. 4h and Supplementary Fig. 25). In addition, the overdamped discharge characteristics of the SLZ15-RRP ceramic were investigated using a specially designed circuit with a 100 Ω resistor at various temperatures under an electric field of 500 kVcm−1. The overdamped oscillation waveforms and discharge energy storage performance are displayed in Supplementary Fig. 26. In a high-temperature environment, the discharged energy density (Wd) can still maintain over 90.0% of this value under the same voltage conditions. The stable Wd of ~ 6.0 Jcm−3 and fast discharge time (t0.9) of ~ 44 ns also indicate the thermally stable discharge performance (Fig. 4i). These results demonstrate the promising potential of the SLZ15-RRP ceramic for high-temperature energy storage applications.

The MLCCs, which were fabricated with five effective dielectric layers using SLZ15 ceramic powder, exhibit a well-defined layered structure and sharp dielectric-electrode interfaces, as shown in the cross-sectional microstructure (Fig. 5a). Evidently, no discernible elemental interdiffusion is observed between the dielectric and electrode layers, indicating excellent chemical compatibility during co-firing. During the process of steadily increasing electric field up to breakdown field, the SLZ15-MLCCs still displays an extremely slim P-E loops, as show in Fig. 5b. The Pmax increases steadily, whereas the Pr remains nearly a constant (below 0.9 μCcm−2). As the electric field increases steadily, it allows the SLZ15-MLCCs to attain the Wrec of 19.0 Jcm−3 at 1050 kVcm−1, and the η remains remarkably high (~95.5%), as depicted in Fig. 5c, which is notably superior to most of the current reported lead-free MLCCs (Fig. 5d and Supplementary Table 1) 28,41–49. To evaluate practical reliability, cyclic stability tests were conducted under 700 kVcm−1. After 106 cycles, neither the Wrec nor the η exhibits significant degradation (Fig. 5e and Supplementary Fig. 27), which confirms that the excellent cycling endurance is suitable for long-term operation. Notably, the SLZ15-MLCCs exhibit excellent stability over broad ranges of frequency and temperature. The variations in its P-E loops are negligible over a temperature range of 25–160°C and a frequency range of 1–100 Hz (Supplementary Figs. 28 and 29a). Meanwhile, it maintains a Wrec of over 10.0 Jcm−3 and an η of over 95.0% within these ranges, with the variation rate of the energy storage performance being less than 6.0% (Fig. 5f and Supplementary Fig. 29b). The excellent cycling, frequency, and temperature stability of the SLZ15-MLCCs fully confirms their significant potential for practical deployment.

It is well known that ceramic dielectric capacitors exhibit excellent energy storage performance at high temperatures, closely linked to variations in their crystal structures 50. As the temperature increases, the simulated P-E loops in Fig. 5g show a slight decrease in Pmax, which is consistent with the above experimental results. This trend can be attributed to the gradual reduction in domain size and dielectric constant with rising temperature. Furthermore, the structural characteristics of the SLZ15 ceramic were evaluated using XRD and Raman spectroscopy from 25°C to 200°C, as shown in Fig. 5h, i and Supplementary Fig. 30. The number and relative intensity of XRD diffraction peaks remain consistent across the temperature range, and the (111) and (200) diffraction peaks shift towards lower angles due to thermal expansion without splitting, indicating the stability of phase structure. Meanwhile, as shown in Fig. 5h, the SLZ15 ceramic exhibits nearly diffuse Raman patterns with consistent peaks over a broad temperature range. These results suggest that the crystal structure remains stable within the tested temperature range, providing the structural characteristics of excellent high-temperature energy storage performance.

In summary, guided by phase-field simulations, this work presents an effective strategy for enhancing the capacitive energy storage of lead-free ceramics by designing weakly coupled polar nanoclusters in superparaelectric state. Atomic-scale HAADF-STEM and polarization mapping reveal nanostructured polar clusters with R- and T-phases that are embedded within a nonpolar C-phase matrix, forming weakly coupled polar nanoclusters. As a result, the SLZ15-MLCCs exhibit large Pmax, high applied electric field and negligible polarization hysteresis, leading to ultra-high energy storage density (Wrec ≈ 19.0 Jcm−3) and near-ideal efficiency of 95.5% at room temperature. In addition, the weakly coupled and disordered polar nanoclusters remain stable at thermal fluctuations, ensuring remarkable high-temperature energy storage performance. When the temperature rises to 160°C, its Wrec remains above 10.0 Jcm−3, and the η reaches as high as over 95.0%. Additionally, the SLZ15-MLCCs also exhibit excellent frequency stability and cyclic stability, and the variations in Wrec and η both remain less than 5.0%. This work establishes a paradigm for achieving ultra-high comprehensive energy storage performance, addressing the critical need for dielectric capacitors in high-temperature environments.

---

## Methods

Sample preparation
The (1-x)[0.65BaTiO3-0.35(Na0.5Bi0.5)TiO3]-xSr0.7La0.2ZrO3 (x=0, 0.05, 0.1, 0.15, 0.2) was fabricated by raw powders of BaCO3 (99.9%), TiO2 (98.0%), Na2CO3 (99.8%), Bi2O3 (99.0%), SrCO3 (99.0%), La2O3 (99.99%), and ZrO2 (99.0%) through a conventional solid-state reaction. The weighed raw materials were ball-milled for 24 h with ethanol, dried at 100°C for 3 h, and subsequently calcined at 850°C for 4 h. The calcined powders were further ball-milled for 24 h with ethanol. After drying, the powders were pre-pressed into 12 mm diameter pellets for cold isostatic pressing. The samples can be obtained by sintering at 1200–1270°C for 4 h.

Repeated rolling processing
The SLZ15-RRP ceramic was fabricated by a repeated rolling processing (RRP) technique, employing pre-sintered SLZ15 powder as the raw material. The pre-sintered SLZ15 powder was initially subjected to ball-milling to refine its particle size and then homogeneously mixed with an organic binder (e.g., PVA) at a mass ratio of 2:1 (powder to binder). The mixture was subjected to 1000 rolling cycles at room temperature under a pressure of 10 MPa to form uniform ceramic tapes. These tapes were then punched into discs (12 mm diameter) and calcined at 650°C for 12 h to remove the binder. Finally, the discs were embedded in presintered powder of the same composition and sintered at 1165°C for 2 h using a double-crucible configuration.

MLCCs fabrication
The SLZ15 ceramic powder with optimal performance was selected as the raw material and thoroughly mixed with an organic vehicle composed of methyl ethyl ketone, butyl benzyl phthalate, polypropylene carbonate, and triolein. After dispersion using a high-speed homogenizer, a uniform and stable ceramic slurry was prepared. Subsequently, the slurry was cast into smooth and continuous green ceramic tapes via a tape casting machine. After drying, platinum paste was coated on the surface of the green tapes as internal electrodes by screen printing. The green tapes with internal electrodes were cut into sheets of specified size, stacked in an alternating alignment mode of internal electrodes, and dense lamination was achieved through isostatic pressing technology. Finally, the laminated green body was sintered at 1220°C in an air atmosphere for 3 h to obtain the SLZ15-MLCCs. After the external electrodes were encapsulated on the SLZ15-MLCCs by silver paste coating, the electrical performance tests were conducted. The overlapping area of two adjacent platinum electrodes in the sintered SLZ15-MLCCs was measured to be 1.7 × 1.6 mm2, and the average thickness of dielectric layer was approximately 8 μm.

Structure characterizations
The phase structure was measured using X-ray diffraction (XRD, D8 Advanced, Bruker, Germany) with Cu Kα radiation. Raman spectra were obtained using a Raman scattering spectrometer (HR800, HORIBA Jobin Yvon, France). The micromorphology of the samples was recorded with a field-emission scanning electron microscope (SEM, S-4800, Hitachi, Japan), and the grain size was evaluated using a combination of the NanoMeasurer software. An atomic-resolution high-angle annular dark-field scanning transmission electron microscope (HAADF-STEM, Titan Themis G2, FEI, USA) was employed to investigate the polar nanoclusters in the ceramics.

Electric property measurements
The P-E loops reported in this study were measured using a FE analyzer (Premier II, Radiant, USA) with a bipolar triangular waveform. The charge/discharge performance of samples was evaluated using a commercial charge-discharge device (CFD-001, Gogo Instruments Technology, China). The dynamic response of the domains to external electric fields was examined using piezoelectric force microscopy (PFM, MFP-3D, Asylum Research, USA).

Phase-field simulations
The details of the phase-field simulation regarding the domain structure and polarization configuration are provided in the Supplementary Information.

## Paper

## Abstract

Ceramic capacitors, although promising for advanced high-power energy storage, face challenges in energy density and efficiency at high temperatures, which restrict their practical applications. Guided by phase field simulations, we propose a structural design strategy to construct weakly coupled polar nanoclusters in superparaelectric state, and fabricate BaTiO3-based multilayer ceramic capacitors via prototype device technology. The capacitors achieve an ultra high energy storage density of 19.0 J·cm-3 and a high energy storage efficiency of 95.5% at room temperature. More importantly, both metrics are still on the order of >10.0 J·cm-3 and >95.0%, respectively, over 25-160 oC, outperforming previously reported ceramic capacitors. The weak coupling between adjacent nanoclusters caused by disordered polar configurations, suppresses nonlinear polarization response and temperature sensitivity, ultimately enabling superior energy storage performance, which is confirmed by atomic-scale microstructure analysis. This work advances next-generation electronics and provides insights for developing high-performance high-temperature ceramic capacitors.

---

## Introduction

Lead-free ceramic capacitors have emerged as a key component for applications in portable electronics, electric vehicles, and large-scale energy storage systems due to their significant advantages, including eco-friendliness and ultra-high power density, which enable ultra-fast charging and discharging rates, as well as high voltage tolerance and reliability 1–3. However, compared to batteries and electrochemical capacitors, relatively low recoverable energy density (Wrec) and efficiency (η) limit their potential to meet practical requirements for miniaturization and integration 4–6. In order to meet the requirements of practical applications, ceramic dielectric capacitors must feature extremely slim polarization-electric field (P-E) loops and high field-induced polarization 7,8. However, achieving high polarization often leads to significant hysteresis effects, and vice versa 9,10. In response to this challenge, researchers employed various strategies to engineer the transition from ferroelectrics (FEs) to relaxor ferroelectrics (RFEs) and have made significant progress 11,12. This transition destroys the long-range ordered, strongly coupled micron-scale FE domains, resulting in lower polarization switching energy barriers and enhanced η value of ceramic capacitors 13,14. According to numerous reported ceramic systems, the BaTiO3-x(Na0.5Bi0.5)TiO3 (0≤x≤1, BT-100xNBT) RFEs have attracted significant attention due to its significant tetragonal distortions with varying composition and high spontaneous polarization 15–17. For instance, through precise local structural design in BT-50NBT-based RFEs, an exceptionally high energy density (>10 Jcm−3) and energy efficiency (>90%) have been achieved 18. Unfortunately, the Wrec value of this ceramic at a high temperature of 150°C is sharply decreased to approximately 8.5 Jcm−3, and the corresponding η is also reduced to around 85%. Temperature-sensitive energy storage performance and low high-temperature capacitance density (<10 Jcm−3) of recently reported lead-free ceramics still restrict their applicability at high-temperature conditions. For instance, the (Bi1/3Na1/6K1/6Ba1/6Sr1/6)(Ti0.8Zr0.2)O3 high-entropy ceramic exhibits an excellent energy storage density of 18.7 Jcm−3 at room temperature. However, its energy storage density notably drops below 10.0 Jcm−3 at 160°C 19. Similarly, the BaTiO3-(Bi0.5Na0.5)(Zn1/3Nb2/3)O3 system formed by multi-ion doping has an ultra high energy storage efficiency of 96.1%, but the insufficient thermal stability of energy storage density limits its applicability in a wide temperature range 20. Therefore, developing lead-free ceramic dielectric capacitors with high energy storage performance and excellent high-temperature stability is crucial for the next generation of dielectric capacitors that can operate stably under high electric fields and at temperatures up to 150°C.

Typical RFEs always exhibit small polarization hysteresis while suffering from early polarization saturation under sufficiently high external electric fields, restricting the rapid enhancement of energy storage performance when increasing the external electric field 21. Moreover, the energy storage performance of typical RFEs is often sensitive to temperature changes 22. From a thermodynamic perspective, domain size plays a crucial role in influencing the polarization response, encompassing long-range FE interactions and switching barriers. When sufficiently reducing the domain size and weakening the domain coupling, the polar state becomes easily redirectable, resulting in nearly zero polarization hysteresis and mitigated polarization saturation. Interestingly, as shown in Fig. 1a, this phenomenon can be observed in superparaelectric state within the temperature range of Tm < T < TB, where Tm is the peak temperature of the dielectric constant and TB represents the Burns temperature. In comparison to strongly coupled micro-domains and nano-domains, weakly coupled polar nanoclusters in superparaelectric state exhibit a super-fast and reversible response under loading and unloading the external electric field, which prevents the phenomenon of polarization hysteresis and premature polarization saturation, resulting in remarkable energy storage density and efficiency 21,23. In addition, these weakly coupled polar nanoclusters are insensitive to the variation of ambient temperature, and the corresponding dielectric constant remains stable over a broad temperature range, which is highly important for enhancing the thermal stability of energy storage performance 24,25.

Guided by phase-field simulations, as shown in Fig. 1b, the introduction of foreign ions such as Sr2+, La3+, and Zr4+ into the BT-35NBT matrix increases the local random field, disrupting long-range ordered, strongly coupled micro-domains and forming small weakly coupled polar nanoclusters. This configuration features rhombohedral (R) and tetragonal (T) polar nanoclusters embedded within cubic (C) paraelectric matrixes. Adjusting the ratio and distribution of polar and nonpolar states for R-, T-, and C-phases aims to minimize polarization hysteresis while maximizing maximum polarization. Such weakly coupled polar nanoclusters can exert a pinning effect that effectively inhibits local structural changes induced by atomic thermal vibration and thereby significantly enhances the stability of the phase structure over a wide temperature range. It is encouraging that the unique structural design enables the fabricated multilayer ceramic capacitors (MLCCs) to exhibit excellent energy storage performance not only at room temperature, but also over a wide temperature range. Even at a high temperature of 160°C, the Wrec remains greater than 10.0 J·cm-3, and the η exceeds 95.0%. This advancement provides a significant reference for developing next-generation high-temperature dielectric capacitors.

---

## Results

To uncover the underlying origin of the enhanced high-temperature energy storage performance of lead-free ceramic dielectrics induced by weakly coupled polar nanoclusters, the two-dimensional phase field simulation was used to study the correlation between the polar structure evolution and the corresponding hysteresis behavior of (1−x)[0.65BaTiO3-0.35(Na0.5Bi0.5)TiO3]-xSr0.7La0.2ZrO3 (SLZ100x, x=0, 0.05, 0.1, 0.15, 0.2) ceramics at different temperatures, as shown in Fig. 2a and Supplementary Fig. 1. The initial BT-35NBT ceramic features long-range ordered, strongly coupled T-phase domain structure, as substantiated by its P-E hysteresis loops with large polarization but high hysteresis loss. After introducing SLZ, as expected, the domains were transformed from macroscopic FE domains to nanodomains and subsequently to smaller weakly coupled polar nanoclusters, accompanied by increasingly slender P-E loops. This progression suggests that the introduction of SLZ effectively disrupts the long-range FE order in BT-35NBT ceramics. Simultaneously, the content of the T-phase decreases significantly, resulting in a disordered polarization structure with coexisting R-, T- and C-phases. The randomly distributed polar structure modifies local energy barriers, stabilizes the favorable polarization, and forms the unique structures with weakly coupled R and T polar nanoclusters divided by nonpolar C-phase over a broad temperature range, thereby enhancing temperature-insensitive energy storage performance. In addition, the weak coupling characteristic is responsible for excellent electric field response performance in the SLZ15 ceramic (Fig. 2b). In the initial state, benefiting from such a weak coupling effect, the polarization directions are highly randomly distributed. Upon the loading of external electric field, the polarizations rapidly reorient and align with the electric field direction. After the removal of external electric field, the polarization quickly deviates from the directional alignment state and eventually recovers its initial disordered distribution, demonstrating fast and reversible polarization response behavior. At the same time, optimizing the ratio and distribution of polar nanoclusters further reduces potential barriers for domain switching, enabling the flattest domain switching paths (Fig. 2c). Weakly coupled polar nanoclusters also promote the formation of random fields, which provides a strong driving force for the electric field-induced recovery of large domains to a multi-domain state (Fig. 2d). These results lead to a recoverable electric field-induced relaxor FE state and promote linear-like polarization behavior.

An aberration-corrected scanning transmission electron microscope was employed to investigate the atomic-scale structural characteristics of SLZx ceramics. Figure 3a, b shows the high-angle annular dark-field scanning transmission electron microscopy (HAADF-STEM) images for representative compositions of BT-35NBT and SLZ15 ceramics along [100]c direction. The polarization displacement vectors were computed through software simulation and presented by yellow arrows. Herein, the morphological structure is identified by observing the projected displacements of the B-site cations (Zr/Ti) relative to the four nearest A-site cations (Ba/Na/Bi/Sr) at the lattice center. Based on the 2D Gaussian peak fitting results, the larger domains can be observed by same arrow pointing for BT-35NBT ceramics (highlighted by the green arrow at the right of Fig. 3a). By contrast, local fluctuations are observed for the SLZ15 ceramic due to the disordered nature of the A-site cations. As a result, smaller weakly coupled polar nanoclusters of R- and T-phases are embedded within nonpolar C-phase matrixes (Fig. 3b). These results confirm that SLZx ceramics with weakly coupled polar nanoclusters were successfully fabricated under the guidance of phase-field simulations. The disordered and weakly coupled polar nanoclusters contribute to enhancing the stability of local structure and energy storage performance under temperature fluctuation 26. Additionally, as observed in the atomic-resolved energy-dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) mapping for the SLZ15 ceramic in Supplementary Fig. 2, the Ba, Bi, Na, La, and Sr elements are distributed in A-sites, while the Zr and Ti elements are distributed in B-sites, respectively. It promotes the destabilization of cation sites in the perovskite structure and induces the formation of weakly coupled polar nanoclusters. From the comparative distribution of pixel intensities of A- and B-site atomic columns between the BT-35NBT and SLZ15 ceramics, it can be concluded that multi-element doping significantly enhances the atomic-scale disorder of the ceramics (Fig. 3c–f). Significantly, the intensity fluctuation is more prominent at the A-site columns (Ba2+/Na+/Bi3+/Sr2+/La2+) in the SLZ15 ceramic, suggesting large random displacements of A-site cations. These random shifts directly generate strong local electric fields that disrupt long-range polar order. In contrast, the B-site (Ti4+/Zr4+) columns show small intensity variations. Nevertheless, their fluctuations exhibit high spatial correlation closely linked to cooperative displacements of B-site cations and tilting of oxygen octahedra. This correlated B-site behavior locally biases polarization directions and contributes to stabilizing nanoscale polar nanoclusters. According to the axial displacement data, the polarization angle and amplitude mapping of BT-35NBT and SLZ15 ceramics along the [100]c direction is illustrated in Supplementary Fig. 3. Compared to the BT-35NBT ceramic, the polarization angle and amplitude of the SLZ15 ceramic exhibit a markedly non-uniform random distribution. Meanwhile, this random distribution of T- and R-phase polar nanoclusters is isolated by nonpolar C-phase, facilitating a more rapid and efficient response to the external electric field 27. In addition, compared with the average c/a ratio of the BT-35NBT ceramic, that of the SLZ15 ceramic displays a noticeable decrease accompanied by a more pronounced discrete distribution (Supplementary Fig. 4). The variation of the c/a ratio indicates that as SLZ content increases, atomic disorder within the system escalates and lattice distortion intensifies, further enhancing the random field and effectively delaying polarization saturation 28.

X-ray diffraction (XRD, Supplementary Fig. 5) analysis confirms that all samples exhibit a pure perovskite phase. The pure BT-35NBT ceramic displays a characteristic T phase, evident from the distinct splitting of XRD peaks (002)/(200) 28,29. As the SLZ content increases, the (200) diffraction peak gradually shifts to a low angle, primarily due to the larger radius of the dopant ions (R(Sr2+)=1.44 Å, R(La3+)=1.06 Å, R(Zr4+)=0.79 Å), which results in lattice expansion. To further analyze the phase composition in the SLZx ceramics, Rietveld refinement was performed on the XRD data for each composition, as shown in Fig. 4a and Supplementary Fig. 6. The results indicate that the rhombohedral (R3c) and tetragonal (P4bm) phases coexist in the SLZ15 ceramic, with mass fractions of 56.2 wt% and 43.8 wt%, respectively. Notably, as the SLZ content increases, the proportion of the R-phase at room temperature increases monotonically, from 24.6 wt% at x=0.05–71.4 wt% at x=0.20. Both the R-phase and T-phase are polar phases with high polarization, which facilitates the achievement of a larger maximum polarization (Pmax) in ceramic dielectrics under the application of an external electric field 23.

To primarily confirm the designed SLZx ceramics in superparaelectric state near room temperature, the temperature dependence of dielectric constant and dielectric loss (tanδ) was analyzed (Supplementary Figs. 7 and 8). As the SLZ content increases, the tanδ exhibits a significant decreasing trend while remaining consistently below 0.01 across a broad temperature range from room temperature to 300°C, accompanied by the shift of Tm towards low temperatures from 184°C for x=0 to −83°C for x=0.20 at 1 kHz. Additionally, the relaxor diffusion factor γ, calculated using the modified Curie-Weiss law 30, tends to increase with the increment of x, indicating an improvement in relaxor properties (Supplementary Fig. 9). Based on the dielectric spectrum at 1 kHz, a possible composition-temperature phase diagram was constructed (Fig. 4b). The Tm significantly decreases with increasing SLZ content, facilitating the transition from relaxor FE to superparaelectric state. Consequently, the designed ceramics are fully situated in superparaelectric state from −56°C to 162°C when x=0.15, indicating the existence of weakly coupled polar nanoclusters over a broad temperature range. In addition, weakened coupling between the R-phase and T-phase polar nanoclusters significantly reduces the stress required for polarization reorientation in response to an external electric field, leading to lower strain vibration and potential failure risks 8,31.

The relaxation characteristics of SLZx ceramics were studied through the first-order reversal curve (FORC) distribution, as shown in Fig. 4c and Supplementary Fig. 10. The BT-35NBT ceramic displays a high-intensity distribution near the origin, indicative of strongly coupled FE domain switching at low electric fields, resulting in an overall increase in polarization 32. This inhomogeneous FORC intensity distribution reflects the typical characteristics of strong polarization nonlinearity in FE materials 33. In contrast, the FORC intensity of the SLZ15 ceramic is more uniform distributed across all electric fields, indicating decreased coercive fields, reduced FE nonlinearity, and a more dispersed polarization contribution 34. In addition, the representative samples of BT-35NBT and SLZ15 ceramics were selected to analyze further the dynamic response of domains by piezoelectric force microscopy (PFM) at various voltages and relaxation times (Supplementary Figs. 11 and 12). For the BT-35NBT ceramic, a strong domain-switching signal is observed at a low voltage of 10 V, whereas the domain-switching signal in the SLZ15 ceramic is weak at this voltage but becomes more pronounced with increasing voltage, suggesting that local random fields and highly dynamic polar nanoclusters are present in the SLZ15 ceramic. Weakly coupled polar nanoclusters require a higher electric field to achieve long-range polarization, which explains the reduced polarization saturation observed in the SLZ15 ceramic. Furthermore, after removing the voltage and allowing a relaxation time of 20 min, the BT-35NBT ceramic retains their original remarkable signals, while the domain-switching signals in the SLZ15 ceramic are barely detectable. These results indicate that the introduction of SLZ diminishes the domain size of the BT-35NBT ceramic and induces weakly coupled polar nanoclusters. This structural modulation yields negligible Pr by virtue of rapid reversible polarization response, while concurrently enhancing the overall energy storage performance.

For ceramic capacitors, the breakdown strength (Eb) significantly influences their operating electric field and energy storage density. Thus, the breakdown characteristics of SLZx ceramics were initially evaluated using the Weibull distribution function 35. All samples exhibit a linear relationship with a large shape parameter (β>10, Supplementary Fig. 13), indicating the reliability of the results and consistent quality of the ceramic samples. In fact, the Eb of ceramic dielectrics is influenced by various complex factors, such as band gap (Eg), grain size, and insulation properties 36,37. For SLZx ceramics, the Eg is significantly enhanced with increasing the SLZ content (Supplementary Fig. 14). Specifically, the values of Eg are enhanced monotonously from 3.12 eV for the SLZ5 ceramic to 3.18 eV for the SLZ20 ceramic, leading to a substantial increase in the Eb. In addition, the average grain size (Ga) and Eb exhibit a negative correlation in ceramic dielectrics 28,38. According to the measured SEM (Supplementary Fig. 15), the Ga was evaluated by NanoMeasurer software. The Ga exhibits a decreasing tendency, from 0.72 μm for the BT-35NBT ceramic to 0.43 μm for the SLZ20 ceramic. The smaller Ga is beneficial to achieving higher Eb. Despite the fact that the radius of impedance spectra for SLZx ceramics tends to decrease with increasing temperature, the higher SLZ content still contributes to a larger radius, indicating the enhancement of total resistivity and Eb at high temperatures (Supplementary Fig. 16). In addition, the distinct single peaks of Z” and M” can be observed for the BT-35NBT ceramic, but they do not coincide at the same frequency (Supplementary Fig. 17). This lack of overlap indicates electrical inhomogeneity. In contrast, the peaks of Z” and M” closely overlap at the same frequency for the SLZ15 ceramic, demonstrating that the introduction of SLZ into the BT-35NBT ceramic effectively improves the electrical homogeneity. This enhancement in electrical homogeneity also contributes to the increase in Eb 39.

To better evaluate the overall energy storage performance of the designed ceramics, the unipolar P-E loops were measured at their critical electric field (Supplementary Figs. 18 and 19), and the related capacitive energy storage performance of Wrec and η were calculated (Fig. 4d). Despite the Pmax of the BT-35NBT ceramic reaching 37.9 μCcm−2 at a low breakdown strength (Eb = 160 kVcm−1), while the remnant polarization (Pr) is as high as 23.8 μCcm−2, leading to low energy storage density and efficiency (Wrec = 1.7 Jcm−3, η=48.6%, Supplementary Fig. 18). By tailoring the polar nanocluster configuration, the values of Wrec and η were dramatically improved to be on the order of 9.2 ± 0.28 Jcm−3 and 91.6 ± 0.24% at x=0.15. It is due to the fact that the strongly coupled FE order of the BT-35NBT ceramic is disrupted, resulting in the formation of R- and T-phase weakly coupled polar nanoclusters isolated by nonpolar C-phase matrixes, which contributes to the rapid polarization response and slim P-E loops. Nevertheless, when excessive SLZ is introduced (e.g., at x=0.2), the formation of nonpolar C-phase becomes dominant. Consequently, the Pmax value at an electric field of 620 kVcm−1 drops to only 30.5 μCcm−2, and the Wrec ultimately decreases to 7.5 Jcm−3. These results indicate that the generation of weakly coupled polar nanoclusters and the alterations in nanocluster configuration significantly optimize the energy storage performance of lead-free ceramics. Compared to the traditional solid-state reaction process, the method of repeated rolling process (RRP) facilitates the refinement of grain size and enhances sintering uniformity, leading to the increased Eb of ceramic dielectrics 25,40. Therefore, SLZ15 ceramics were prepared via the RRP (SLZ15-RRP) using SLZ15 powder to further optimize their energy storage performance. Figure 4e illustrates the unipolar P-E loops of the SLZ15-RRP ceramic under different electric fields. Obviously, the Pr remains negligible and its value is as low as 0.9 μCcm−2 even at 780 kVcm−1. It is worth noting that an ultra-high Wrec of 13.6 Jcm−3, along with a near-ideal efficiency of 95.0%, can be achieved for the SLZ15-RRP ceramic. The reliability of the Eb is validated through Weibull distribution analysis, as shown in Supplementary Fig. 20. The β of the SLZ15-RRP ceramic is 17.34, indicating high reliability of the Eb. The calculated Eb is on the order of 782.9 kVcm−1, closely corresponding to the Eb obtained in P-E loops. Herein, the remarkable comprehensive energy storage performance in this study is primarily due to their weakly coupled polar nanoclusters, compact microstructure, and uniform and small grain size (Supplementary Fig. 21). Weakly coupled polar nanoclusters exhibit high sensitivity to external electric fields, which enables ceramic dielectrics to achieve near-ideal energy efficiency. Meanwhile, the refined grain size effectively inhibits electrical tree propagation and shortens their growth paths, thereby significantly enhancing the Eb, as shown in Fig. 4f and Supplementary Fig. 22.

Except for achieving high energy storage performance at room temperature, their stability under different conditions is also critical in practical applications. Therefore, over a broad temperature range from room temperature to 160°C, the P-E loops consistently maintain a slim shape and the variation of Wrec and η is less than 10.0% and 5.0%, respectively, at an electric field of 500 kVcm−1 (Fig. 4g and Supplementary Fig. 23). To further assess frequency adaptability, P-E loops of the SLZ15-RRP ceramic were tested over a frequency range of 1–100 Hz (Supplementary Fig. 24). Obviously, the Wrec remains stably at ~ 7.9 Jcm−3, and the η consistently stays above 94.0%, which indicates excellent frequency stability. Moreover, the energy storage performance of the SLZ15-RRP ceramic remains stable with a change rate of less than 2.0% in both Wrec and η after 106 cycles (Fig. 4h and Supplementary Fig. 25). In addition, the overdamped discharge characteristics of the SLZ15-RRP ceramic were investigated using a specially designed circuit with a 100 Ω resistor at various temperatures under an electric field of 500 kVcm−1. The overdamped oscillation waveforms and discharge energy storage performance are displayed in Supplementary Fig. 26. In a high-temperature environment, the discharged energy density (Wd) can still maintain over 90.0% of this value under the same voltage conditions. The stable Wd of ~ 6.0 Jcm−3 and fast discharge time (t0.9) of ~ 44 ns also indicate the thermally stable discharge performance (Fig. 4i). These results demonstrate the promising potential of the SLZ15-RRP ceramic for high-temperature energy storage applications.

The MLCCs, which were fabricated with five effective dielectric layers using SLZ15 ceramic powder, exhibit a well-defined layered structure and sharp dielectric-electrode interfaces, as shown in the cross-sectional microstructure (Fig. 5a). Evidently, no discernible elemental interdiffusion is observed between the dielectric and electrode layers, indicating excellent chemical compatibility during co-firing. During the process of steadily increasing electric field up to breakdown field, the SLZ15-MLCCs still displays an extremely slim P-E loops, as show in Fig. 5b. The Pmax increases steadily, whereas the Pr remains nearly a constant (below 0.9 μCcm−2). As the electric field increases steadily, it allows the SLZ15-MLCCs to attain the Wrec of 19.0 Jcm−3 at 1050 kVcm−1, and the η remains remarkably high (~95.5%), as depicted in Fig. 5c, which is notably superior to most of the current reported lead-free MLCCs (Fig. 5d and Supplementary Table 1) 28,41–49. To evaluate practical reliability, cyclic stability tests were conducted under 700 kVcm−1. After 106 cycles, neither the Wrec nor the η exhibits significant degradation (Fig. 5e and Supplementary Fig. 27), which confirms that the excellent cycling endurance is suitable for long-term operation. Notably, the SLZ15-MLCCs exhibit excellent stability over broad ranges of frequency and temperature. The variations in its P-E loops are negligible over a temperature range of 25–160°C and a frequency range of 1–100 Hz (Supplementary Figs. 28 and 29a). Meanwhile, it maintains a Wrec of over 10.0 Jcm−3 and an η of over 95.0% within these ranges, with the variation rate of the energy storage performance being less than 6.0% (Fig. 5f and Supplementary Fig. 29b). The excellent cycling, frequency, and temperature stability of the SLZ15-MLCCs fully confirms their significant potential for practical deployment.

It is well known that ceramic dielectric capacitors exhibit excellent energy storage performance at high temperatures, closely linked to variations in their crystal structures 50. As the temperature increases, the simulated P-E loops in Fig. 5g show a slight decrease in Pmax, which is consistent with the above experimental results. This trend can be attributed to the gradual reduction in domain size and dielectric constant with rising temperature. Furthermore, the structural characteristics of the SLZ15 ceramic were evaluated using XRD and Raman spectroscopy from 25°C to 200°C, as shown in Fig. 5h, i and Supplementary Fig. 30. The number and relative intensity of XRD diffraction peaks remain consistent across the temperature range, and the (111) and (200) diffraction peaks shift towards lower angles due to thermal expansion without splitting, indicating the stability of phase structure. Meanwhile, as shown in Fig. 5h, the SLZ15 ceramic exhibits nearly diffuse Raman patterns with consistent peaks over a broad temperature range. These results suggest that the crystal structure remains stable within the tested temperature range, providing the structural characteristics of excellent high-temperature energy storage performance.

In summary, guided by phase-field simulations, this work presents an effective strategy for enhancing the capacitive energy storage of lead-free ceramics by designing weakly coupled polar nanoclusters in superparaelectric state. Atomic-scale HAADF-STEM and polarization mapping reveal nanostructured polar clusters with R- and T-phases that are embedded within a nonpolar C-phase matrix, forming weakly coupled polar nanoclusters. As a result, the SLZ15-MLCCs exhibit large Pmax, high applied electric field and negligible polarization hysteresis, leading to ultra-high energy storage density (Wrec ≈ 19.0 Jcm−3) and near-ideal efficiency of 95.5% at room temperature. In addition, the weakly coupled and disordered polar nanoclusters remain stable at thermal fluctuations, ensuring remarkable high-temperature energy storage performance. When the temperature rises to 160°C, its Wrec remains above 10.0 Jcm−3, and the η reaches as high as over 95.0%. Additionally, the SLZ15-MLCCs also exhibit excellent frequency stability and cyclic stability, and the variations in Wrec and η both remain less than 5.0%. This work establishes a paradigm for achieving ultra-high comprehensive energy storage performance, addressing the critical need for dielectric capacitors in high-temperature environments.

## Methods

Sample preparation
The (1-x)[0.65BaTiO3-0.35(Na0.5Bi0.5)TiO3]-xSr0.7La0.2ZrO3 (x=0, 0.05, 0.1, 0.15, 0.2) was fabricated by raw powders of BaCO3 (99.9%), TiO2 (98.0%), Na2CO3 (99.8%), Bi2O3 (99.0%), SrCO3 (99.0%), La2O3 (99.99%), and ZrO2 (99.0%) through a conventional solid-state reaction. The weighed raw materials were ball-milled for 24 h with ethanol, dried at 100°C for 3 h, and subsequently calcined at 850°C for 4 h. The calcined powders were further ball-milled for 24 h with ethanol. After drying, the powders were pre-pressed into 12 mm diameter pellets for cold isostatic pressing. The samples can be obtained by sintering at 1200–1270°C for 4 h.

Repeated rolling processing
The SLZ15-RRP ceramic was fabricated by a repeated rolling processing (RRP) technique, employing pre-sintered SLZ15 powder as the raw material. The pre-sintered SLZ15 powder was initially subjected to ball-milling to refine its particle size and then homogeneously mixed with an organic binder (e.g., PVA) at a mass ratio of 2:1 (powder to binder). The mixture was subjected to 1000 rolling cycles at room temperature under a pressure of 10 MPa to form uniform ceramic tapes. These tapes were then punched into discs (12 mm diameter) and calcined at 650°C for 12 h to remove the binder. Finally, the discs were embedded in presintered powder of the same composition and sintered at 1165°C for 2 h using a double-crucible configuration.

MLCCs fabrication
The SLZ15 ceramic powder with optimal performance was selected as the raw material and thoroughly mixed with an organic vehicle composed of methyl ethyl ketone, butyl benzyl phthalate, polypropylene carbonate, and triolein. After dispersion using a high-speed homogenizer, a uniform and stable ceramic slurry was prepared. Subsequently, the slurry was cast into smooth and continuous green ceramic tapes via a tape casting machine. After drying, platinum paste was coated on the surface of the green tapes as internal electrodes by screen printing. The green tapes with internal electrodes were cut into sheets of specified size, stacked in an alternating alignment mode of internal electrodes, and dense lamination was achieved through isostatic pressing technology. Finally, the laminated green body was sintered at 1220°C in an air atmosphere for 3 h to obtain the SLZ15-MLCCs. After the external electrodes were encapsulated on the SLZ15-MLCCs by silver paste coating, the electrical performance tests were conducted. The overlapping area of two adjacent platinum electrodes in the sintered SLZ15-MLCCs was measured to be 1.7 × 1.6 mm2, and the average thickness of dielectric layer was approximately 8 μm.

Structure characterizations
The phase structure was measured using X-ray diffraction (XRD, D8 Advanced, Bruker, Germany) with Cu Kα radiation. Raman spectra were obtained using a Raman scattering spectrometer (HR800, HORIBA Jobin Yvon, France). The micromorphology of the samples was recorded with a field-emission scanning electron microscope (SEM, S-4800, Hitachi, Japan), and the grain size was evaluated using a combination of the NanoMeasurer software. An atomic-resolution high-angle annular dark-field scanning transmission electron microscope (HAADF-STEM, Titan Themis G2, FEI, USA) was employed to investigate the polar nanoclusters in the ceramics.

Electric property measurements
The P-E loops reported in this study were measured using a FE analyzer (Premier II, Radiant, USA) with a bipolar triangular waveform. The charge/discharge performance of samples was evaluated using a commercial charge-discharge device (CFD-001, Gogo Instruments Technology, China). The dynamic response of the domains to external electric fields was examined using piezoelectric force microscopy (PFM, MFP-3D, Asylum Research, USA).

Phase-field simulations
The details of the phase-field simulation regarding the domain structure and polarization configuration are provided in the Supplementary Information.

3. How does the ionic substitution specifically alter the Burns temperature (T ) and B contribute to the stabilization of the superparaelectric state?
Our reply:
Thank you for raising this insightful question regarding the role of ionic substitution in modulating the Burns temperature (T ) and stabilizing the B superparaelectric state. We have further clarified the underlying mechanisms in the revised manuscript.
In general, T denotes the onset of the formation of PNRs and corresponds to the B temperature below which dynamic dipolar correlations can be observed (Nano Energy 2019, 58, 768; Solid State Commun. 1983, 48, 853). Ionic substitution, especially with the cations of varying sizes and charges, introduces random fields and local disorder, which disrupt the long-range ferroelectric order (Rare Met. 2022, 42, 399-405). This disorder suppresses the characteristic temperature at which polar correlations appear, thus lowering T For instance, when Zr⁴⁺ substitutes Ti⁴⁺ at the B-site, its smaller B. ionic radius and equal valence preserve charge balance but cause local lattice distortions. Similarly, co-doping of Sr²⁺/La³⁺ at the A-site brings about cation size mismatch and slight charge variance, further strengthening random fields. These combined effects decrease the energy scale necessary for PNRs nucleation, shifting T B downward, often towards or below room temperature, which is favorable for temperature-stable dielectric behavior.
Ionic substitution accomplishes directional control of T and stabilizes the B superparaelectric state through the targeted modification of the host lattice, functioning via two synergistic mechanisms. Firstly, by exploiting the differences in ionic radius and valence between dopants and host ions, ionic substitution accurately reconstructs the lattice field and induces BO octahedral distortion. This directly 6 regulates the activation energy barrier for polarization fluctuations (J. Am. Chem. Soc. 2023, 145, 11764-11772; Nat. Commun. 2024, 15, 6754), allowing T to be shifted B towards or close to room temperature and thereby establishing the thermodynamic precondition for superparaelectric stability within the application temperature range. Secondly, ionic substitution simultaneously introduces chemical disorder and facilitates grain refinement, confining polar domains to the nanoscale (3-5 nm). This effectively disrupts long-range ferroelectric order and transforms the polarization response from domain-wall-dominated displacement to the dynamic relaxation of nanoscale polar clusters (Ferroelectrics 1987, 76, 241-267; Appl. Phys. Lett. 2024, 124, 090501). The weakened inter-cluster coupling and enhanced pinning effects from random fields further decouple polarization dynamics, broadening the relaxation spectrum and expanding the superparaelectric state.
Ionic substitution systematically reduces the temperature T by introducing the B disorder, which suppresses long-range polar order. Simultaneously, it stabilizes the superparaelectric state via enhanced PNR pinning, weakened inter-cluster coupling, and a broadened energy landscape. These factors collectively contribute to the temperature-insensitive and frequency-stable dielectric properties in relaxors.

2-3 Basic and Conceptual Questions for Authors
1. What defines the threshold between “weakly coupled” and “strongly coupled” domains from a physical perspective (energy barrier, correlation length, or permittivity variance)?
Our reply:
Thank you for your valuable comment. The demarcation between weakly and strongly coupled domains is defined by two core physical parameters: polarization correlation length and polarization switching energy barrier. These parameters can be directly observed and quantified via advanced microscopic and electrical characterization techniques.
First, the polarization correlation length reflects the spatial scale within which adjacent polarization units maintain directional consistency. As depicted in Fig. R16 (Original Fig. 3), strongly coupled domains exhibit long-range order with highly consistent polarization vectors (yellow arrows), forming continuous tetragonal-phase domains without phase isolation. In contrast, weakly coupled domains display randomly distributed polarization vectors, where rhombohedral-phase and tetragonal-phase polar nanoregions are isolated by a non-polar cubic-phase matrix, with each polar nanoregions being merely 1-2 nm in size. The absence of spatial correlation between adjacent polar nanoregions, along with the physical isolation provided by the cubic matrix, significantly reduces the correlation length, which is a defining spatial characteristic of weak coupling.
Second, the polarization switching barrier determines the energy requisite for domain reorientation. Piezoresponse force microscopy (PFM) results (Figs. R17 and R18, Original Supplementary Fig. 10 and Fig. 11) disclose that strongly coupled samples show a distinct and persistent switching signal even at low voltages (10 V), which remains stable after 20 minutes, indicating high energy barriers and a propensity towards frozen polarization states. Conversely, weakly coupled samples exhibit minimal response at 10 V. A substantial switching signal emerges only above 30 V and decays almost entirely within 20 minutes after voltage removal. This demonstrates that weakly coupled domains switch and relax rapidly with low energy barriers, facilitating highly reversible polarization dynamics.
In summary, the boundary between weak and strong coupling domains is physically delineated by a short correlation length (generally < 5 nm) and low switching energy barriers in weakly-coupled systems, as opposed to a long correlation length and high barriers in strongly-coupled systems. These characteristics jointly account for the narrow hysteresis, high reversibility, and temperature-insensitive performance in our designed relaxors. In this ceramic, weakly coupled polar nanoregions facilitate efficient energy storage with minimal loss.

2. How does the nanocluster coupling influence the local potential landscape for polarization reversal?
Our reply:
Thank you for your insightful comment. The coupling strength between polar nanoclusters fundamentally determines the local potential energy landscape for polarization reversal.
In strongly-coupled systems, the deep energy wells give rise to the formation of high barriers that necessitate collective switching (Nat. Commun. 2024, 15, 8651; Energy Environ. Sci. 2017, 10, 528-537). In contrast, in weakly coupled systems, such as the SLZ15 ceramic, the potential landscape is fragmented, shallow, and spatially isolated, which allows for independent and low-barrier polarization switching of individual polar nanoclusters. This mechanistic framework directly accounts for the polarization evolution observed in our work.
In the initial state, the weak-coupling characteristic of the SLZ15 ceramic leads to highly random polarization orientations. Since each polar nanocluster is located in its own shallow, isolated potential well, achieving complete polarization alignment is difficult under zero field. Upon an external electric field, these shallow potential wells enable the polar nanoclusters to align rapidly and reversibly along the direction of the electric field, while the resistance between the clusters is extremely small. After the removal of electric field, the polarization can rapidly revert to its initial disordered distribution state, owing to the absence of strong coupling effects, deep level traps, and any collective energy barrier that would maintain the aligned state (Nat. Commun. 2025, 16, 2892; Energy Environ. Sci. 2023, 16, 4511-4521). Therefore, the entire polarization evolution process, from random distribution to electric field-induced alignment, and then to the rapid restoration of the disordered state, directly demonstrates how weakly coupled polar nanocluster structures dominate the switching dynamics. It is thus confirmed that the designed local potential landscape, characterized by shallow and fragmented wells, not only promotes a highly reversible polarization response but also supports the superior energy storage efficiency and temperature stability in the SLZ15 system.

3. What role does entropy play in stabilizing the disordered superparaelectric configuration?
Our reply:
Thank you for raising this profound question. The term entropy, a core thermodynamic quantity characterizing the number of accessible microscopic states such as ions, atoms, and phase regions, plays a crucial role in stabilizing disordered superparaelectric configurations (Mater. Today 2024, 77, 92; InfoMat. 2023, 5, e12488). An increase in structural disorder is associated with a larger number of accessible microscopic configurations, which leads to an elevation in the entropy (ΔS) of the system. Based on the free-energy relation ΔG=ΔH TΔS, the increase in entropy can counterbalance the enthalpy gain related to long−-range order, rendering the disordered state thermodynamically favorable across a wide temperature range (Nat. Mater. 2022, 21, 1074-1080; Prog. Mater. Sci. 2024, 145, 101300).
In this work, for SLZ-modified ceramics, entropy-mediated stabilization is achieved through specific structural mechanisms. The multi-component ions (Sr2+, La3+, Zr4+) are randomly distributed, enhancing configurational disorder and lattice distortion due to differences in ionic radii and valence states. This generates strong local random fields that disrupt the long-range tetragonal (T) order, leading to the coexistence of rhombohedral (R) and tetragonal (T) polar nanodomains embedded in a non-polar cubic (C) matrix. The resulting multiphase nanoclusers exhibits high mixing entropy, which thermodynamically favors the persistence of this weakly coupled, spatially heterogeneous structure across a broad temperature range. Consequently, the entropy-stabilized disordered configuration directly mitigates the destabilizing effects of thermal fluctuations. By maintaining dynamic polar nanoregions while preventing them from merging into static macroscopic domains, the system retains narrow hysteresis, high reversibility, and temperature-insensitive energy storage performance based on the designed superparaelectric state. Therefore, entropy is not only a statistical result of the disordered state, but also an active thermodynamic driving force, which helps to design high-performance relaxor ferroelectric dielectrics with excellent thermal stability.
